title: The spider that builds an underwater lung
hook: An underwater spider builds an air bell. But how does it keep breathing?
paper_title: The diving bell and the spider: the physical gill of Argyroneta aquatica
citation: Seymour & Hetz (2011), Journal of Experimental Biology 214:2175–2181
summary: The diving bell spider makes a silk-supported air chamber underwater. Seymour and Hetz measured gas exchange and showed that oxygen diffusing from water into bells can meet resting spider demand under their aquarium conditions. Nitrogen loss eventually makes air renewal necessary.
evidence_note: This is a small aquatic-physiology laboratory study of resting spiders and bell gas exchange. The bell's long-term renewal and active/wild limits remain; this is not a claim that spiders never surface.

evidence.design: Physiological laboratory measurements of field-collected Argyroneta aquatica building air bells; bell volume and oxygen partial pressures measured with micro-optodes, compared with respirometry of resting spiders. Fourteen empty bells from eleven spiders were measured for conductance. Warm roughly 25°C still water; no wild trial.

limitations: Resting metabolic rates were investigated; active and wild oxygen needs were not established.
A few small bells did not meet resting oxygen demand; no claim that all bells are self-sufficient.
More-than-one-day renewal estimates rely partly on a gas transfer model, not a directly documented wild dive.
Reference photos are independent natural history images, not the studied spiders; diagrams are qualitative.

editorial_story.audience: Curious non-specialist adults encountering an unfamiliar aquatic spider.
editorial_story.subject: The air-breathing freshwater diving bell spider Argyroneta aquatica.
editorial_story.setting: Freshwater vegetation and the separate warm laboratory aquaria that supplied measured gas-exchange evidence.
editorial_story.opening_context: The opening photo and first sentence identify the spider underwater and the air chamber; the mystery is how the gas stays breathable.
editorial_story.normal_expectation: An isolated bubble has finite oxygen and a spider needs oxygen, so it appears that frequent surfacing should be required.
editorial_story.story_selection: A visually identifiable spider and clear physically plausible diffusive exchange give a compact surprising mechanism, avoiding an abstract methods recap.
editorial_story.decisive_limit: Dissolved oxygen in the water can maintain resting spider metabolism in tested conditions, not an indefinite supply to active or all wild spiders; nitrogen leakage still requires renewal.
editorial_story.question: Why does a diving bell spider's underwater chamber remain breathable longer than a simple trapped air pocket?
editorial_story.why_it_matters: Shows how an air-breathing freshwater animal can exploit an interface with dissolved oxygen, and why physical context changes breathing ecology.
editorial_story.narrative_arc: Named spider and underwater air room; construction of the bell; finite-air puzzle; dissolved oxygen entering from water; original optode study; resting-supply evidence; nitrogen loss; laboratory scope; return to spider.
editorial_story.closing_payoff: The water outside the bubble helps resupply oxygen to the air inside, but an air trip is still eventually needed.

posts.caption:
How does a spider breathe underwater?

The diving bell spider (*Argyroneta aquatica*) builds a web-supported pocket of air under freshwater. It replenishes the pocket from the surface, but the remarkable part is what happens between those trips: oxygen dissolved in the surrounding water can diffuse into the bell. That makes the air-water boundary a **physical gill**.

Seymour and Hetz measured oxygen and gas conductance in laboratory diving bells. Many bells supplied enough oxygen for resting spiders in warm, still aquarium water. But nitrogen leaves the chamber, so it gradually shrinks and the spider still needs fresh air eventually. These tests do not establish oxygen supply during all activity or in every natural habitat.

TT-006 | Seymour & Hetz (2011), Journal of Experimental Biology, DOI: 10.1242/jeb.056093
Full source, methods, limitations and media credits: https://akshaymohan16.github.io/toxic-tales-library/sources/tt-006.html

Real spider reference photographs (not the experiment): bykovskii and Lennart Lennuk, CC BY 4.0, cropped/graded; source/licence links on research page. Gas-transfer and measurement sequences are original conceptual illustrations, not recorded data. Synthetic narration. Official Toxic Tales logo.
